title: Hockey World Cup | India survives England’s onslaught, advances to the next round
content:
It was not the way they would have wanted, but it would just be fine. They made it harder for themselves, but the Indian women survived an onslaught from England to hold on for a nervy goalless draw on Thursday and progress to the World Cup second round.
The sun, for a change, shone on the Wagener Stadion as the Indian team basked in a rare moment of success on this stage. In a pool (D) where India (five points) was ranked the third-best side, Sjoerd Marijne’s outfit finished second behind China (seven points).
It was a superb rearguard effort from the Indian defence with England needing just one goal to break the resistance and with that, the rival’s hearts.
In the final minute, Tessa Howard struck at goal, but Bichu Devi sprung to her left to push the ball away, making India believe again. It was a remarkable save.
Her jubilant senior goalkeeping partner Savita Punia called it the “save of the match”.
Savita did her part, too, keeping England at bay in the third quarter with two superb saves. But the European side came harder in the final 15 minutes, including removing its goalkeeper for an extra outfielder. England had 16 circle penetrations to India’s two in the second half as the latter was retreating into its own quarter of the pitch.
Nerves probably played a part and India kept making errors on the ball, allowing England to dominate possession and accumulate scoring opportunities.
Darcy Bourne and Anna Toman had eight tries from penalty corners in the second period, but India’s PC defence was superbly led by skipper Salima Tete, who rushed out to frustrate them repeatedly.
India had chances to make its life easy in the first half but Navneet Kaur and Deepika were wasteful with their finishing from short corners. Navneet fired wide from her second attempt, and became predictable with her drag-wide-and-strike approach as Miriam Pritchard guessed it right.
Ultimately, it didn’t prove costly for India. But Marijne’s side will need to do better against the Netherlands in the second-round game on Friday.

title: Duleep Trophy | Venue change an acknowledgement that domestic cricket needs audience
content:
On Duleep Trophy matchdays at the BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) on the outskirts of Bengaluru last year, there was a familiar sight. A small group of enthusiastic fans would gather near the gates, hoping to watch some of the country’s finest domestic cricketers in action.
But more often than not, they were left disappointed. Security personnel would bluntly tell them that spectators were not allowed inside. The fans would linger for a while and try their luck but would reluctantly walk away eventually. On one occasion, a person claiming to be a player’s relative had to make several phone calls and wait for hours before finally being permitted entry.
It was an odd situation for a tournament of the Duleep Trophy’s stature.
This is not an isolated instance. When Karnataka hosted Kerala in a Ranji Trophy match at the Alur grounds here, spectators eager to catch a glimpse of Sanju Samson were not allowed.
That is why the BCCI’s decision to move this season’s Duleep Trophy final from the CoE to Chennai’s M.A. Chidambaram Stadium, specifically to accommodate fans, is more than just a change of venue. It is a welcome acknowledgement that domestic cricket needs an audience.
When BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia was asked why spectators could not attend the matches, he said that the Board would consider moving the final. Around 10 days later, it did just that.
Crowd presence does more than enliven the stands. A cheer can provide an emotional lift to players in the often unsung setting of First Class cricket.
The Duleep Trophy may not have the glamour of the IPL or international cricket, but for generations of players, it has been a significant stepping stone to the National team.
The fans deserve to be a part of the journey.

title: Table Tennis | Tanishka, Prateek clinch U-15 titles in National Ranking tournament
content:
Tanishka Kalbhairav of Karnataka and Maharashtra’s Prateek Tulsani began the new season on a winning note, claiming the under-15 girls’ and boys’ titles respectively at the UTT National Ranking Table Tennis tournament at The Sportz Hub on Thursday.
In an entertaining final, 14-year-old Tanishka staged a spirited comeback against West Bengal’s Saturya Banerjee to prevail 9-11, 13-11, 7-11, 11-6, 11-6. Trailing 1-2 and with Saturya’s backhand topspins initially proving too hot to handle, Tanishka found her range with a succession of forehand winners to pocket the winner’s purse of ₹22,400.
Prateek, having had a disappointing run last season, also reigned supreme. The lanky Thane paddler overpowered West Bengal’s promising left-hander Rajdeep Biswas in straight games (11-6, 11-9, 11-9). Rajdeep, who had bowed out in the u-13 semifinals a day earlier, found Prateek’s onslaught too difficult to withstand.
The victory marked an encouraging start to the season for Prateek, who trains under Rajendra Sawant in Thane. After emerging as the National u-13 champion in 2024, he struggled to make the transition to the u-15 category last season. On Thursday, he underlined his potential by topping the National Ranking tournament.

title: HOCKEY WORLD CUP | India enters the next round with a mountain to climb
content:

For skipper Harmanpreet Singh, the game against Pakistan felt like ‘playing in India’ as he was serenaded by the large number of expats after his two goals in the 5-3 win on Wednesday.

title: England vs Pakistan 1st Test: Robinson, Tongue take 5 wickets each as host dominates on Day 1
content:
England's post-Bazball era got off to an encouraging start on a dominant Day 1 of the first Test against Pakistan, with pacers Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue each taking five wickets to rip through the tourists' batting lineup at Headingley.
After Pakistan collapsed from 117-3 to 171 all out, England made inroads in the evening session Thursday to reach the close on 112-2 and was trailing by just 59 runs.
It could hardly have gone any better for Joe Root, who was beginning his second stint as captain following the retirement of Ben Stokes and was there at stumps on 37 not out alongside Jordan Cox (23 not out) after winning the toss under an overcast sky.

Asked which of the bowlers was keeping the match ball, Tongue revealed after the close of play that it was being shared — literally.
“The groundsman has kindly split the ball in half so I'm sure I'll be able to get that mounted somewhere at home,” said Tongue, who claimed his fourth five-wicket haul in his 13th Test. “It's crazy — it's the first time I've seen that happen.”
For Robinson, it was another dramatic return. He was playing his first Test since June at Lord's, where he took a match-winning 7-77 against New Zealand in his first Test in two years. A knee injury and doubts about his fitness prevented his return in that series that England lost 2-1, leading to the retirement of Stokes and the firing of Brendon McCullum as Test coach.
Pakistan, with just two wins in its last seven Tests and missing captain Babar Azam (finger injury), provided ideal opponents for the start of England's latest reset and lost its last five wickets for 21 runs in 22 balls.
“They bowled very well, we have to give credit to the England bowlers. They were decent with their length and they were hitting the right spots,” Imam said.
“Obviously we have to work hard now but I always believe that it's a long game... things change very quickly. Get two wickets and the game's going to change.”
In England's reply, Mohammad Abbas trapped Ben Duckett for 15 and Emilio Gay departed for 33, nicking Mohammad Ali to second slip, but Root and Cox settled the home side.
Root, in particular, looked in prime form and has already hit six fours in his 53-ball knock early in his chase for a 42nd Test century.
Pakistan, which hasn't won a Test series in England since 1996, had Salman Agha deputising as skipper with Babar not recovering from a finger injury.

According to the BBC, it is the first time a team has taken a wicket off the first ball of a Test series in England, which has been hosting matches since 1880.
